Hogwash means something that is complete nonsense — a statement, claim, argument, or idea that is so wrong, so foolish, or so untrue that it is not even worth taking seriously. When you call something hogwash, you are saying it deserves to be thrown out entirely, not debated.

It is not a mild disagreement. Calling something hogwash is a strong, blunt dismissal. You are essentially saying: "This is garbage. It has no value. I refuse to give it any respect."
What Kinds of Things Get Called Hogwash?

Hogwash is used for a wide range of worthless or dishonest content:

  • False claims — A company claims their pill will make you 10 years younger overnight. That's hogwash.
  • Weak, poorly reasoned arguments — Someone gives an excuse that doesn't hold up to the slightest questioning. That's hogwash.
  • Exaggerated boasting — A politician claims he single-handedly saved the economy. Hogwash.
  • Conspiracy theories or wild, baseless beliefs — "The moon is made of cheese." Pure hogwash.
  • Empty, meaningless talk — A speech full of impressive-sounding words that ultimately say nothing and mean nothing. Total hogwash.

The common thread is this: hogwash has no real substance. It might sound convincing or be presented confidently, but when you examine it, there is nothing real or truthful holding it up.

This is important to understand: hogwash is not a neutral word. It carries a strong emotional tone of contempt and dismissal. The person using it is not just saying "I disagree." They are saying "this is so obviously wrong or stupid that I won't waste time analyzing it."

There is also a slightly colorful, folksy quality to the word. It sounds like something a plain-spoken, no-nonsense person would say — someone who has no patience for lies or foolishness. Because of this, the word can sometimes carry a faint touch of humor, even while being a serious dismissal.

Hogwash sits in the middle range of dismissive words — it is strong, but not the harshest thing you can say. It is more colorful and emphatic than simply saying "nonsense," but it is not rude or vulgar in the way that some stronger words are. You could say it in polite company, in a newspaper column, or in a heated conversation, and it would fit all three.

Think of it on a scale:
"I'm not sure I agree" → "That's wrong" → "That's hogwash" → "That's utter garbage"

Hogwash lands firmly on the dismissive end, but it has a certain spirited, almost old-fashioned character that keeps it from sounding purely aggressive.

Hogwash is an informal word. You would not use it in an academic paper or a formal legal document. It belongs in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Opinion writing (columns, editorials, blogs)
  • Speeches where someone wants to sound direct and plain-spoken
  • Arguments and debates where you want to forcefully dismiss something

It is more common in American English than British English, and it has a slightly old-fashioned feel — it is not slang that teenagers invented last year. It has been around a long time and carries that old, sturdy, reliable quality. This makes it feel trustworthy and direct, rather than trendy.

It is worth knowing that hogwash is also commonly used as a one-word exclamation — someone says something outrageous, and you simply respond: "Hogwash!" This is the noun being used in the same way you might say "Nonsense!" It is the same meaning, just used as a sharp, spoken response.

• "Everything he said in that interview was complete hogwash — not a single fact checked out."
  • "Don't listen to that hogwash about miracle diets. There is no shortcut."
  • "The report was full of hogwash dressed up in scientific-sounding language."
  • "She saw through his hogwash immediately and walked out of the meeting."
  • "I've heard a lot of hogwash in my life, but that takes the prize."
How It Differs from Similar Words

A few words share territory with hogwash, but each has its own flavor:

  • Nonsense — General and neutral. Hogwash is stronger and more colorful.
  • Balderdash — Very similar to hogwash in tone and feel; also old-fashioned and emphatic. The two are nearly interchangeable.
  • Rubbish — Common in British English; hogwash is the American counterpart.
  • Baloney / Bunk — Also American, informal, and dismissive. Slightly milder and more casual than hogwash.
  • Drivel / Twaddle — These suggest content that is tediously worthless — boring, rambling nonsense. Hogwash feels more actively wrong or dishonest, not just dull.
  • Claptrap — Refers especially to empty, showy talk meant to impress. Hogwash is broader.
Hogwash is an informal American English noun meaning complete nonsense — something so false, foolish, or baseless that it deserves nothing but dismissal.
